I covered all 21 verses, but some only thinly. My tool limit ran out before I could finish Gill (his text stopped partway through v. 13) or read the Ellicott and Pulpit commentaries on each verse. So vv. 13, 15–17 and 19–20 rest on just one or two sources. A few labels such as "Reformed" or "Calvary Chapel / Pentecostal list" are my own way of grouping writers by their tradition. The pages themselves don't use those labels.

## Joel 3: Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1: "in those days… when I restore Judah"**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word).** "Those days" continues the "afterward" of Joel 2:28. That means the broad "last days" which began with Jesus' ascension and Pentecost. The return from Babylon fulfilled this in a smaller, immediate way. The full fulfilment is an end-times regathering of Israel, leading to Israel's national salvation (Romans 11:26–27). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/
- **Gill.** Kimchi applied the verse to the Messiah's times. Gill denies it refers to Babylon or to earlier captivities, because what follows in the chapter didn't happen after those returns. He sees it as the Jews' present scattering and a future restoration to their land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html

**v. 2: Valley of Jehoshaphat**
- **Where is it?** Writers disagree, and this disagreement runs through the whole chapter:
  - **A symbol, not a real place (Clarke, Guzik).** Clarke says no valley of that name exists in Judea, so the name must be symbolic. "Jehoshaphat" means "the LORD judges." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-2.html. Guzik agrees and calls it God's place of judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/
  - **Gill** lists several options: Kidron, or the Valley of Berachah where King Jehoshaphat won his victory. He thinks no ordinary place name is meant, only a place named after the judgment God carries out there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
  - **Barnes** suggests the picture may borrow from Jehoshaphat's deliverance in 2 Chronicles 20. He also notes a tradition that Christ will come down to judge over this valley. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-2.html
  - **Constable:** the place where Yahweh judges, with no particular site meant. Valleys were common battlefields. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joel-3.html
  - **Bible Hub's study page** leans the other way. It favours the Kidron Valley and says Zechariah 14:3–4 supports a literal site. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/joel/3.htm
- **Who are "My people"?** Guzik says the verse is mainly about how the nations treat Israel, but it also covers how they treat the church. God takes mistreatment of His people personally. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/. Gill applies it to converted Jews and also to "all the saints" who suffered under antichrist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html

**v. 3: lots cast, a boy for a prostitute**
- **Gill** gives two readings: the children were handed over for sexual use, or they were simply used as payment for a prostitute and for wine. Either way the point is lust, drunkenness and how cheaply the captives were valued. He links it to the Romans enslaving 97,000 Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Guzik:** it is bad to treat any human life as cheap, and worse to treat God's people as cheap. God remembers and will repay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 4: Tyre, Sidon, Philistia**
- **Gill:** these were close neighbours and bitter enemies of the Jews. God asks why they treat Him and His people this way, and promises quick, sudden payback. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Guzik:** God practically dares the nations to come against Him. Judgment, God giving people what they deserve, is the one part of His plan that is "plainly logical." Grace is not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 5: silver, gold and treasures taken to their temples**
- **Gill:** the treasures are either the goods of God's people or the temple's vessels. He says it isn't certain that any of them ever reached Tyre's temples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html

**v. 6: sold to the Greeks**
- **Gill:** Ezekiel 27:13 shows that Tyre traded in human beings, with Javan (Greece) among its customers. Selling captives far away meant they could not easily be bought back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Bible Hub's study page** says later inscriptions at Tyre show Greek slave markets, which explains the reference. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/joel/3.htm

**v. 7: "I will rouse them"**
- **Gill** lists the views. Some see fulfilment when Alexander and his successors freed Jewish captives. Others see a future return of the Jews. Gill prefers the gathering of the spiritual Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html

**v. 8: sold to the Sabeans**
- **Gill:** some think this was literally fulfilled when Alexander took Tyre and sold about 30,000 of its people as slaves, some into Jewish hands. The Sabeans were a distant people of Arabia Felix. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Precept Austin:** the enslaved become the enslavers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-3-commentary
- **Guzik** cites Trapp's list of the bad ends met by Roman emperors who persecuted Christians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 9: "Prepare for war"**
- **Gill:** heralds announce war to the nations. He mostly reads it as mockery of God's enemies, though it could be meant seriously as encouragement to God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Guzik:** God challenges the nations to prepare for war against Him. They will one day do it (Revelation 16), and God laughs at them (Psalm 2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 10: plowshares into swords; "let the weak say, I am strong"**
- **Gill** notes this reverses Isaiah 2:4. He says Paul applies the idea to spiritual weakness (2 Corinthians 12:10). Even the weakest believer is strong in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Guzik:** this is "positive thinking" aimed at God, and it is useless. Your arms are too short to box with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 11: "Bring down Your mighty ones, O LORD"**
- **Gill:** a prayer. Kimchi, Aben Ezra and many others take the "mighty ones" as angels. Gill prefers Christ's armies of Revelation 19:14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **JFB** gives one translation note: "assemble" may mean "hasten" (Maurer). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/joel-3.html

**v. 12: "there I will sit to judge"**
- **Gill:** God speaks here, answering the prayer of v. 11. The picture is a judge sitting on the bench and then carrying out the sentence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Does "roused" mean resurrection?** JFB notes Abarbanel saw a hint of the dead being woken for judgment (compare Job 14:12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/joel-3.html. William Kelly rejects that. He says the scene is a judgment of living nations at a literal place, not the great white throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-2.html

**v. 13: sickle and winepress**
- **Constable** compares Isaiah 63 and Revelation 14:14–20. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joel-3.html
- **Guzik** says Revelation 14 uses the same winepress picture for Jesus' judgment at Armageddon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 14: "valley of decision"**
- **Guzik:** evangelists often use the phrase to mean that *you* must decide for Christ. Joel means the opposite: God does the deciding. So decide for Jesus now, so that you never stand in that valley. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/
- **Constable** agrees it is God's decision about the nations' fate. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joel-3.html
- **Gill:** it is the same valley as Jehoshaphat. The Vulgate reads "valley of concision." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Other readings.** The Catholic Encyclopedia gives "valley of destruction." https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/valley-of-josaphat. The Biblical Illustrator keeps the call to personal decision, applied to the Spirit's work in a soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/joel-3.html

**vv. 15–16: darkened sky; "the LORD will roar from Zion"**
- **Guzik:** this returns to the cosmic signs of Joel 2:30–31. Through it all, the LORD is His people's shelter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/
- **Matthew Henry:** the Hebrew word means "harbour," a refuge and home for God's people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_003.cfm

**v. 17: Jerusalem holy, never overrun again**
- **Guzik:** God restores both His people and His city to glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

**v. 18: wine, milk, and a spring from the LORD's house**
- **Literal or spiritual?** Shittim lies beyond the Jordan, where no stream from the temple could naturally reach. So several commentators read the spring as a picture:
  - **Clarke and Barnes** both say this. Clarke links it to Ezekiel 47 and the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-18.html
  - **Gill:** the spring is the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/3-18.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Christ is the fountain. Gospel grace will reach the far-off, barren Gentile world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-18.html
- **Calvin:** God's blessing will spread even into desert valleys. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment2/v1.0/harry/comm_vol27/htm/iii.iv.xvi.htm
- **Guzik:** waters flowing in the millennium (Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 14:8). Shittim was where Israel both sinned (Numbers 25) and set out to conquer (Joshua 3). God's grace covers both the failure and the victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/
- **Simeon:** the spring must have a spiritual meaning, so the whole passage describes the millennium. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/shh/joel-3.html

**v. 19: Egypt and Edom**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** some take this as the blood of Jewish captives or refugees killed in Egypt and Edom. It recalls Shishak's attack. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joel/3.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Jews who fled to them for safety were killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-21.html

**v. 20: Judah inhabited forever**
- **Matthew Henry:** the church of Christ will continue until the end of time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_003.cfm
- **Coffman:** God's covenant people will always exist. It is no guarantee for any political state, Israel included. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/joel-3.html

**v. 21: "avenge" or "cleanse" their blood?**
- **Translation is the main issue here:**
  - **Barnes:** the verb means "pronounce innocent." By punishing the killers, God declares the victims' blood innocent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/3-21.htm
  - **Clarke:** God will avenge His martyrs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-21.html
  - **Ellicott** leans toward God pardoning those not yet pardoned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/3-21.htm
  - **Got Questions:** both ideas are true. Israel is forgiven, and God avenges them. https://www.gotquestions.org/bloodguilt.html
- **Guzik and Clarke** compare the closing words "the LORD dwells in Zion" with Ezekiel's "The LORD is there." Clarke sees both as Christ's continuing presence with His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**1. Is the chapter about the end times, and does it apply to Israel or the church? (vv. 1–2, 9–17, 20)**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** calls applying it to the last judgment "too strained." He dismisses the idea of the whole world gathering in this valley as a superstition from a time when sound teaching had been lost. For him the point is that God protects the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-2.html
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel; Enduring Word is on your Pentecostal list):** Armageddon, Matthew 25 read as a judgment on how nations treat Israel, and a millennium. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-3/. Chuck Smith even guesses the valley will be the new one formed when the Mount of Olives splits (Zechariah 14). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-2.html
- **Precept Austin:** strongly insists the land promises are "not a promise to the church." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-3-commentary
- **Gill (Baptist):** a future conversion of the Jews. He reads Tyre and the "heathen" as stand-ins for "Papists and Turks." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joel-3.html
- **Spiritual readings:**
  - Matthew Henry: the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_003.cfm
  - Coffman: no guarantee for any political state. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/joel-3.html
  - William Kelly takes the opposite position: it is not the church at all, but God's earthly people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-21.html

**2. v. 21 applied to the Christian life**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** mentions the "avenging martyrs" reading. He also mentions applying it to elect people not yet called. His main point is two things: guilt still felt on the conscience, and sin that remains in believers, which God will one day remove completely. He insists the old nature never improves. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/perfect-cleansing
- **Benson Commentary** (my label: early Methodist): full pardon *and* "entire sanctification." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/3-21.htm. Compare that with Spurgeon's view that sin remains until glory.
- **Calvin:** God must wash away His people's sins before He can be their Redeemer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/3-21.html

I found nothing specifically Lutheran or Anglican on this chapter.

## Other views

**Catholic**
- **The valley.** The Catholic Encyclopedia gives two options: Berachah, about 11 miles from Jerusalem, or a symbolic "valley of judgment." From the 4th century, Christians, Jews and later Muslims placed the last judgment in the Kidron Valley. Early Jewish tradition denied the valley was a real place. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/valley-of-josaphat
- **The chapter as a whole.** The Encyclopedia's article on Joel describes it as Israel's redemption carried out as judgment on the Philistines, Phoenicians, Edomites and Egyptians. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08419a.htm
- **When was Joel written?** The same article mentions two views. One dates Joel to King Josiah's time. Later scholars date it after the Exile, partly because ch. 3 assumes the Jews are already scattered. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/joel
- **v. 21.** Calmet, as quoted by Benson, reads it as the new law's sacrament cleansing what the old law could not. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/3-21.htm

**Modern scholarship and Bible dictionaries**
- The ISBE article at netbible.org calls the identification with Berachah "improbable." It says Kidron is a ravine (*nachal*) rather than a broad valley (*ʿemeq*). Joel may have meant an ideal spot. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Jehoshaphat%2C+Valley+of&theme=wiki
- Utley says Shittim can't be the literal target in v. 18, so the verse is a picture of plentiful harvests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/joel-3.html

**Not found:** Orthodox readings, Bible Odyssey articles, verse notes from the NET Bible itself, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace use of this chapter.
